source.title: Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding
source.authors: Dan Hendrycks; Collin Burns; Steven Basart; Andy Zou; Mantas Mazeika; D. Song; Jacob Steinhardt

record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream benchmark accuracy across model sizes, a different measure bearing on V6. It does not measure the loss or compute-optimal allocation in the original scaling-law claim.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates downstream accuracy, not held-out cross-entropy loss, compute, or parameter-token allocation. Its discussion of the Kaplan scaling result is cited background, not a result from this study. The benchmark is text-only; its discussion of multimodal understanding does not report a multimodal experiment. Table 1's discipline and average results are included separately below.
record.test_reason: The study reports multitask benchmark accuracy for GPT-3 at four sizes (2.7B to 175B) and UnifiedQA at several sizes. That bears on V6, whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale. It fits no loss curves and does no compute or allocation analysis, so V1 to V5 and V7 are untested. The Kaplan 10x-model/5x-data statement is cited background, not a result of this study.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors find that models up to 13B are at chance, while 175B GPT-3 reaches 43.9%. They say size is key but fine-tuning also helps, since 11B UnifiedQA beats 175B GPT-3. They also note that progress on this test is less steady than on prior benchmarks, and that it is unclear whether simply scaling up will solve it. Their main conclusions are about lopsided performance, poor calibration, and weakness on calculation, law and morality, not about scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates multiple-choice downstream accuracy rather than fitting held-out pretraining-loss curves or optimizing parameters and tokens under a compute budget.
record.method_sensitivity: GPT-3 accuracy monotonically increases with the number of few-shot examples, according to Figure 10. The paper also says UnifiedQA accuracy declines by several percentage points if the </s> input marker is removed.
record.problems: The study does not measure loss or compute, and its downstream scaling comparisons cover selected model sizes and a single benchmark. GPT-3's first three reported few-shot averages are close to chance and not monotonic. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the accuracy results.
record.rows_left_out: No table results relevant to V6 were left out. Per-task accuracy values shown only in Figure 6 and Appendix Figure 9 are not individually transcribed because the flattened figure text does not reliably assign exact values to each model and task.

untested.parts: Prediction of downstream accuracy from pretraining loss; any fitted trend or extrapolation; tasks beyond this one benchmark.
All: text-only benchmark, no loss-law fits in other regimes.

missing.what: Fine-tuned RoBERTa-base (125M) 27.9%, ALBERT-xxlarge (223M) 27.1% and GPT-2 (1.5B) 32.4%, against UnifiedQA 60M at 29.3% and 3B at 43.7%. The authors attribute the gaps to pretraining dataset size rather than parameter count, which bears on whether scale in parameters alone predicts downstream accuracy.

Figure 1b: GPT-3 accuracy by size on HellaSwag and SuperGLUE versus this test. It shows continuous gains on the older benchmarks but a jump only at the largest size on this one. The older-benchmark curves come from Brown et al., so this is partly a cited result.

record.verdict_notes: V6 is tested only as accuracy against model size on one benchmark, with four GPT-3 sizes. The flat-then-jump pattern is the study's main bearing on V6. Random-baseline rows r1 to r5 are unlinked. The UnifiedQA support verdict is weak: there are three points and the models are fine-tuned. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law fits in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute comparisons or parameter/token allocation results.
No controlled comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No experiments on other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer as tests of the same loss-law form.
Tests downstream accuracy on this benchmark across selected model sizes and settings, not predictability across downstream tasks generally or prediction from pretraining loss.
No comparison of scaling-law fitting methods, exponents, parameter-count conventions, training schedules, or curve shapes.

relationships.condition: GPT-3 few-shot and zero-shot, 2.7B to 13B parameters
relationships.reason: Average accuracy stays at chance and is non-monotonic (25.9%, 24.9%, 26.0%) across a ~5x parameter increase, with zero-shot around 25% (r10, r15, r20, r30). Per-discipline rows (r6 to r9, r11 to r14, r16 to r19) show the same pattern.
relationships.display_finding: Few-shot accuracy varied nonmonotonically at 25.9%, 24.9% and 26.0% across roughly 5× parameter growth, while zero-shot accuracy stayed around 25%, with similar patterns across disciplines.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: GPT-3 few-shot and zero-shot, 2.7B to 13B parameters
source_check.reason: Few-shot averages remain near chance at 25.9%, 24.9% and 26.0% (r10, r15, r20); smaller-model zero-shot accuracy is around 25% (r30). Increasing size produces no consistent improvement in this range.

relationships.reason: Accuracy jumps to 43.9% few-shot and about 37.7% zero-shot only at 175B (r25, r29; disciplines r21 to r24). The authors contrast this with the steadier gains on other benchmarks, so improvement with scale holds but is not predictable from smaller sizes.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy jumps to 43.9% few-shot and about 37.7% zero-shot only at 175B, preventing reliable prediction from smaller sizes.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Substantial gains appear only at the largest tested size: 43.9% few-shot and about 37.7% zero-shot (r25, r29). Section 4.2 and Figure 1b contrast this pattern with steadier improvements on earlier benchmarks, qualifying predictable improvement across sizes.

relationships.condition: UnifiedQA (T5-based, fine-tuned QA, transfer evaluation) at 60M, 3B and 11B
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises from about 29.3% to 43.7% to 48.9% with size (r26, r27, r28). There are only three points, and no fit is reported.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased from about 29.3% to 43.7% to 48.9%, although three measurements without a fitted curve establish only a directional trend.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: UnifiedQA (T5-based, fine-tuned QA, transfer evaluation) at 60M, 3B and 11B
source_check.reason: Transfer accuracy increases across the three reported sizes: approximately 29.3%, 43.7% and 48.9% (r26, r27, r28), supporting improvement with scale in this setting.
